Not sure where to start?

What is troubling your eyes?

Pick whatever sounds closest. We will point you to the right place to start. This is a guide, not a diagnosis.

Choose what sounds closest to your problem

Cloudy or dim vision

A good place to start Cataract

One common reason is a cataract (मोतियाबिंद), where the lens inside the eye turns cloudy. It is more likely as people get older. Other eye problems can look similar, so a proper check comes first.

Next step: Book an eye check. The doctor looks at the lens with a slit lamp and tells you what is causing it.

Book a check-up Read about cataract

A child's eyes not looking straight

A good place to start Squint

When one eye turns in, out, up or down, it is called a squint (भेंगापन). In children it can lead to a lazy eye if it is left alone, so it is worth getting it checked early.

Next step: Bring your child in for an eye check. Depending on what the doctor finds, glasses, patching or an operation may help.

Book a check-up Read about squint Read about amblyopia

Living with diabetes

A good place to start Diabetic Retinopathy

Diabetes can damage the retina (आँख का पर्दा) at the back of the eye, often before you notice any change in your sight. That is why people with diabetes are asked to have their retina checked regularly.

Next step: Book a retina check. You may get drops that widen the pupil and blur your vision for a few hours, so come with someone and do not drive back.

Book a check-up Read about diabetic retinopathy

Wanting to be free of glasses

A good place to start ICL (Implantable Collamer Lens)

For people with high power or a thin cornea, an ICL may be an option. It is a thin lens placed inside the eye. Not everyone is suitable, and that can only be decided after your eyes are measured.

Next step: Book a check-up for ICL. The doctor measures your eyes and tells you honestly whether it suits you.

Book a check-up Read about ICL

A baby born early

A good place to start ROP (Retinopathy of Prematurity)

Babies born early can develop ROP, a problem with the blood vessels of the retina. It does not show from outside, so the eyes need to be screened by an eye doctor.

Next step: Ask your baby's doctor when the eye screening is due, then call us to book it.

Book a check-up Read about ROP

Glaucoma or eye pressure in the family

A good place to start Glaucoma

A family history of glaucoma (काला मोतिया) raises your own risk. Glaucoma often gives no early warning, and the damage it causes cannot be reversed, so regular checks matter.

Next step: Book a glaucoma check. It includes an eye pressure test and a look at the optic nerve.

Book a check-up Read about glaucoma

Same daySudden flashes, floaters or a shadow

A good place to start Retinal Detachment

Sudden flashes of light, a shower of new floaters, or a dark curtain over part of your vision can mean the retina (आँख का पर्दा) is pulling away. This needs to be seen by a doctor the same day.

Next step: Call the branch now and tell them what you are seeing.

Call Patna now Read about retinal detachment

A red, watery or painful eye

A good place to start Cornea

This can come from many things, including an infection or injury of the cornea, the clear front of the eye. If it hurts, or your sight drops, do not wait it out.

Next step: Book a visit. If it started after an injury, call the branch first.

What we treat, in plain words

Nine areas of eye care, from a child's first squint check to retina surgery. Each page explains the condition, the signs to watch for and what happens on the day.

  1. 01

    Cataract मोतियाबिंद

    The lens inside the eye turns cloudy, usually with age. A short operation replaces it, and most people go home the same day.

    Read about cataract
  2. 02

    Cornea

    Infections, ulcers, injuries, keratoconus and scars on the clear front window of the eye, up to corneal transplant.

    Read about cornea
  3. 03

    Glaucoma काला मोतिया

    Slow damage to the eye's nerve, often from high eye pressure. There are usually no early signs, so regular checks matter.

    Read about glaucoma
  4. 04

    Diabetic Retinopathy

    Diabetes (शुगर) can harm the retina long before sight changes. A retina check finds it early, when treatment helps most.

    Read about diabetic retinopathy
  5. 05

    Retinal Detachment

    The retina (आँख का पर्दा), the seeing layer at the back of the eye, pulls away. Sudden flashes, floaters or a dark shadow need care the same day.

    Read about retinal detachment
  6. 06

    Squint भेंगापन

    Eyes that do not point the same way, in children or adults. Glasses, eye exercises or a muscle operation can straighten them.

    Read about squint
  7. 07

    Amblyopia Lazy eye

    One eye does not learn to see sharply. Glasses and patching work best when started early in childhood.

    Read about amblyopia
  8. 08

    ICL Implantable Collamer Lens

    A thin lens placed inside the eye for people with high power, so they depend less on glasses. Your eyes are measured first to see if it suits you.

    Read about ICL
  9. 09

    ROP Retinopathy of Prematurity

    An eye problem in babies born early. It cannot be seen from outside, so the baby needs an eye screening by an eye doctor.

    Read about ROP

Our story

Started and run by eye surgeons

Sarvdrishti Eye Hospital was started in 2018 by eye surgeons who trained at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. It is still run by doctors: its three directors are eye surgeons who see patients at our branches.

Their aim was eye care of the standard they trained in, for the whole population of Bihar, without a long journey to reach it. Today there are branches in Patna, Gaya and Hajipur. Between them they look after every part of the eye, from cataract and glaucoma to the retina, the cornea, children's eyes and the eyelids, with a scientific, evidence based approach.

What we treat

Care for every part of the eye

From a child's first eye check to retina surgery. Each area has its own doctors, tests and equipment.

  • Cataract

    Phaco surgery through a very small cut, usually without stitches. Lens choices include trifocal and EDOF lenses, for people who want to depend less on glasses.

    • Cataract

  • Retina

    Laser and injections for diabetic eye disease, surgery through tiny openings for a detached retina, and eye screening for babies born early.

    • Diabetic Retinopathy
    • Retinal Detachment
    • ROP

  • Glaucoma

    Eye pressure and side vision checks, eye drops, laser, and glaucoma surgery (trabeculectomy) when drops are not enough.

    • Glaucoma

  • Cornea

    Infections, ulcers, keratoconus and injuries of the clear front window of the eye, up to corneal transplant.

    • Cornea

  • Children's eyes

    Eye checks for children, glasses, patching for a lazy eye, and squint surgery when it is needed.

    • Squint
    • Amblyopia

  • ICL and contact lenses

    ICL, a thin lens placed inside the eye for high power. Contact lenses too, including special lenses for keratoconus.

    • ICL

  • Eyelids and around the eye

    Droopy eyelids, eyelid surgery, scars, lumps and tumours around the eye, and tear duct problems. This is called oculoplasty.

    • Dr. Rajnee Sinha

  • Eye injuries

    An ocular trauma unit for injuries to the eye. After an injury, call the nearest branch straight away.

Equipment

The machines behind your check-up

What each of the main machines does, in plain words.

  • 01

    OCT scan (Topcon)

    Retina, glaucoma and cornea

    Takes a cross-section picture of the retina, the eye's nerve or the cornea in a few seconds, without touching the eye.

  • 02

    Retinal angiography (Zeiss)

    Retina

    A dye given into a vein in the arm lights up the blood vessels of the retina in photos, to show leaks and blockages.

  • 03

    Humphrey visual field test

    Glaucoma

    Maps the side vision of each eye. Its Glaucoma Progression Analysis compares every test with the ones before, to show whether glaucoma is getting worse.

  • 04

    Retina surgery system (Alcon Constellation)

    Retina surgery

    For operations on the retina and the gel that fills the eye, through openings small enough to often need no stitches.

  • 05

    532 nm green laser

    Retina

    Seals leaking blood vessels and weak spots in the retina, for example in diabetic eye disease.

  • 06

    YAG laser

    Cataract and glaucoma

    Clears the haze that can form behind a lens implant after cataract surgery, and makes a tiny opening in the iris to prevent one type of glaucoma. No cut is needed.

Some tests and operations are done at one branch only. When you book, the branch will tell you where yours takes place.

मोतियाबिंद में आँख का natural lens धीरे-धीरे धुंधला हो जाता है। ये चश्मे या दवा से ठीक नहीं होता। इसका इलाज एक छोटी surgery है, जिसमें धुंधला lens हटाकर नया साफ़ lens लगाया जाता है।

  1. 01

    Doctor आपकी ज़रूरत और budget के हिसाब से lens के options समझाते हैं।
  3. 03
    Stitch-less surgery
    Phaco technique से छोटे से चीरे वाली surgery. टांके नहीं लगते और उसी दिन घर वापसी।
बिना टांके की surgery
Micro Incision Cataract Surgery (MICS), जिसमें healing जल्दी होती है।

Phacoemulsification machines से precise और safe surgery.
Premium lens options
Monofocal, Multifocal, Toric और Trifocal lens उपलब्ध।
उसी दिन घर वापसी
Day-care procedure है, भर्ती होने की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती।

About Dr. Kumar Vivek

Dr. Kumar Vivek is a retina surgeon and one of the directors of Sarvdrishti. He studied medicine at Nil Ratan Sircar Medical College, Kolkata, then did his MD in ophthalmology at Dr. R.P. Centre, AIIMS, New Delhi. He stayed on for three years as a senior resident, training in retina surgery.

Most of his work is on the retina, the thin layer at the back of the eye that senses light. He operates through very small openings (23G, 25G and 27G) that do not need stitches. Amblyopia Lazy eye

Amblyopia, or lazy eye, is when one eye does not develop full sight in childhood, even with glasses, because the brain learns to rely on the other eye. It is very treatable when found early, so every child should have an eye check before starting school.

01What it is

What is amblyopia?

Sight is not fully formed at birth. Through early childhood, the brain learns to see by using clear pictures from both eyes. If one eye sends a blurred or turned picture, the brain starts to ignore it, and that eye never learns to see sharply.

The eye itself often looks normal, and the child does not complain, because the other eye sees well. Many cases are found only when the good eye is covered during a check-up.

Treatment works by making the brain use the weaker eye. It works best in young children and becomes harder after about seven or eight years of age, although older children can still improve.

Common causes

  • A squint, where one eye turns
  • Unequal glasses power between the two eyes
  • High glasses power in both eyes
  • Something blocking sight, such as a cataract in a child or a drooping eyelid

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • Often no sign at all

    The child sees well with the good eye and does not notice anything wrong.

  • An eye that turns

    A squint is one of the most common causes.

  • Upset when one eye is covered

    A child who fusses, pushes your hand away or peeps when the good eye is covered.

  • Tilting the head or squinting

    Shutting or narrowing one eye to see better.

  • Clumsiness

    Bumping into things on one side, or poor judgement of depth.

03How it can look

How it can look

Our Patna branch, as a lazy eye may see it when the good eye is covered. Drag the handle to compare.

04Tests

How we check

  1. 01

    Vision test for each eye

    With pictures, symbols or letters to suit the child's age.

  2. 02

    Glasses power with drops

    Drops relax the eye's focusing so the true power can be measured. They take up to an hour to work.

  3. 03

    Squint check

    Covering each eye in turn to look for a turn.

  4. 04

    Eye health check

    To rule out a cataract, a drooping eyelid or a problem in the retina.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • The first step

    Glasses

    The right glasses, worn all day, are often enough to improve the weaker eye over a few months.

  • Most common

    Patching

    A patch over the stronger eye for some hours a day, usually two to six, makes the weaker eye work. Close work such as drawing or reading during patch time helps.

  • Instead of a patch

    Atropine drops or a filter

    A drop in the stronger eye, or a special filter on its glasses lens, blurs that eye so the weaker eye does more of the work. Useful for children who will not keep a patch on.

  • Where needed

    Treating the cause

    An operation for a childhood cataract, a drooping eyelid that blocks sight, or a squint, along with patching.

Ayushman card and insurance

All three branches accept the Ayushman card (PM-JAY), and cashless treatment works with most insurance TPAs. Call the branch to check what is covered for your treatment.

06On the day

Your child's first visit

  1. 1

    Vision test

    Each eye is tested on its own, with games or pictures for young children.

  2. 2

    Drops

    Drops are put in to measure the true glasses power. Bring a snack and a toy, as they take up to an hour to work.

  3. 3

    Examination

    The doctor checks for a squint, the health of each eye and the glasses power.

  4. 4

    Treatment plan

    You get the glasses prescription and, if needed, a patching plan: how many hours a day, and for how long.

  5. 5

    Follow-up

    Visits every 6 to 12 weeks to check progress and adjust the patching.

07Afterwards

Making treatment work at home

What helps

  • Put the patch directly on the skin, not on the glasses, so the child cannot peep.
  • Make patch time fun: drawing, puzzles, colouring, or reading together.
  • Keep the glasses on all day, every day, unless told otherwise.
  • Tell the teacher, so the child gets support at school.
  • Do not stop patching early once the sight improves. The doctor reduces it slowly, so the eye does not slip back.
  • Keep every follow-up visit.

Call the branch if

  • The skin under the patch becomes sore or broken
  • Your child says the stronger eye has become blurry
  • With atropine drops: a flushed face, fever or unusual restlessness

09Questions

Questions people ask

When should my child's eyes be checked?

An eye check before starting school is a good idea for every child, and sooner if you notice a squint, if lazy eye or squint runs in the family, or if the child was born early.

Is it too late after age 8?

Treatment works best in young children, but older children and even teenagers can improve. It is always worth a check.

How long does treatment take?

Usually several months, sometimes longer. Most children improve steadily with glasses and regular patching.

Can patching harm the good eye?

Not when it is done as advised. The doctor checks both eyes at every visit for this reason.

Do eye exercises or video games help?

Some newer games and programs are used along with patching, but glasses and patching remain the main treatment. Ask the doctor before trying any.

01What it is

What is a cataract?

Behind the coloured part of your eye sits a small, clear lens. It focuses light onto the retina at the back of the eye, a little like the lens of a camera. With a cataract, this lens slowly turns cloudy, so everything you see becomes dull and blurred.

Most cataracts come with age, and nearly everyone has some clouding after 60. They can also come earlier: after an eye injury, with diabetes, after long use of steroid medicines, and rarely from birth.

Glasses help for a while, but they cannot clear a cloudy lens. The only cure is an operation, and there is no need to wait for the cataract to become "ripe". The right time is when it starts to make everyday life harder: reading, cooking, recognising faces or going out after dark.

More likely with

  • Age, especially after 60
  • Diabetes
  • An earlier injury to the eye
  • Long use of steroid tablets, drops or inhalers
  • Smoking
  • Years of strong sunlight without eye protection

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • Blurred or dull vision

    As if you are looking through a dirty or misted window. Colours look faded or yellowish.

  • Glare from lights

    Headlights, the sun or a bulb seem too bright, or have a halo around them.

  • Trouble at night

    Seeing in dim light, or walking and driving after dark, becomes harder.

  • Glasses that keep changing

    You need a new power often, or you suddenly read better without your reading glasses.

  • Double vision in one eye

    You see two of something even with the other eye closed.

  • A white or grey pupil

    In a late cataract the black centre of the eye can look milky. In a child, a white pupil needs an eye check soon.

03How it can look

How it can look

Our Patna branch, as it may look to someone with this problem. Drag the handle to compare.

04Tests

How we check

  1. 01

    Vision test

    Reading letters on a chart, one eye at a time, with and without glasses.

  2. 02

    Slit lamp examination

    The doctor looks at the lens through a microscope with a thin beam of light. This shows how cloudy it is.

  3. 03

    Retina check with drops

    Drops widen the pupil so the doctor can check the retina and the optic nerve. The drops blur your sight for a few hours.

  4. 04

    Eye pressure test

    A quick, painless test for glaucoma, which can be present alongside a cataract.

  5. 05

    Lens measurements

    If you decide on surgery, a scan measures the length and curve of your eye to work out the power of the new lens.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • Early cataract

    Glasses, for now

    In the early stage, a new glasses power and brighter lighting can keep you comfortable for a while.

  • Most cataracts

    Phaco surgery

    Phacoemulsification. The cloudy lens is broken up with ultrasound and removed through a tiny cut that usually needs no stitches. A folded artificial lens (IOL) is placed where it was.

  • Hard or advanced cataracts

    SICS

    Small incision cataract surgery. The lens is removed whole through a slightly larger cut that seals itself. It works well for very hard cataracts.

Choosing your new lens

Before the day, the doctor explains which lens suits your eyes, your work and your budget.

  • MonofocalClear for distance. Most people wear glasses for reading afterwards.
  • ToricAlso corrects cylinder power (astigmatism), for sharper sight without thick glasses.
  • Multifocal, trifocal and EDOFPremium lenses that cover distance and near or middle distance, so you depend less on glasses. They do not suit every eye.

Ayushman card and insurance

All three branches accept the Ayushman card (PM-JAY), and cashless treatment works with most insurance TPAs. Call the branch to check what is covered for your treatment.

06On the day

On the day of surgery

  1. 1

    Before the day

    Your sugar and blood pressure are checked, the lens power is measured, and you are told which medicines to take or stop. Tell the doctor if you take blood thinners.

  2. 2

    When you arrive

    Come with a family member, and follow what you were told about food and medicines. Drops widen the pupil and numb the eye.

  3. 3

    The operation

    It usually takes 15 to 30 minutes. You lie down and stay awake, and should feel no pain. You may see light and movement, but not the instruments.

  4. 4

    Going home

    After a short rest, most people go home the same day, with a shield over the eye and a set of drops.

  5. 5

    The next day

    A quick check of the eye, then follow-up visits over the next few weeks.

07Afterwards

After surgery

What helps

  • Use the drops exactly as prescribed, usually for four to six weeks.
  • Wear the shield while sleeping for about a week, and do not rub or press the eye.
  • Keep water, soap and dust out of the eye for one to two weeks. Wipe your face with a clean, damp cloth instead.
  • Avoid bending low and lifting heavy things for the first week.
  • Reading, watching TV and walking are fine from the first day.
  • Have your glasses power checked after about a month, once the eye has settled.

Call the branch if

  • Pain gets worse instead of better
  • Your sight drops after first getting better
  • The eye becomes more red, sticky or swollen
  • You see a shadow, flashes or many new floaters

09Questions

Questions people ask

Does cataract surgery hurt?

No. The eye is numbed with drops or a small injection, so most people feel only light pressure. The eye may feel gritty for a day or two afterwards.

Do I need to wait for the cataract to ripen?

No. Modern surgery works best before a cataract becomes very hard. The right time is when it starts to affect your daily life.

Will I need glasses afterwards?

With a standard monofocal lens, most people see well at a distance and wear glasses for reading. Toric and multifocal lenses can reduce the need for glasses. The doctor will explain what to expect for your eyes.

Can both eyes be done on the same day?

Usually one eye is done first, and the second a few weeks later, once the first has settled.

Can a cataract come back?

No. The cloudy lens is removed for good. In some people the thin layer behind the new lens turns hazy months or years later. This is cleared with a quick, painless laser treatment (YAG laser) in the clinic.

Can I have surgery if I have diabetes?

Yes, as long as your sugar is under control. The retina is checked before surgery, because diabetes can affect it too.

01What it is

What is the cornea?

The cornea is the clear dome over the coloured part of your eye. It lets light in and does most of the focusing, so it has to stay clear and evenly curved. It is also very sensitive, which is why even a speck of dust hurts.

Because it sits at the front, it takes the most damage: infections, scratches, chemical splashes and dryness. Some problems start from within, such as keratoconus, where the cornea slowly thins and bulges into a cone shape, usually from the teenage years.

Care ranges from a few days of drops to long term treatment. A painful red eye with blurred sight should always be seen quickly, because a corneal ulcer can scar the eye within days.

Cornea problems we treat

  • Corneal ulcers and infections
  • Keratoconus
  • Corneal scars
  • Dry eye and allergic eye disease
  • Pterygium
  • Swelling of the cornea after eye surgery
  • Inherited conditions such as Fuchs dystrophy
  • Injuries, foreign bodies and chemical burns

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • Pain or a gritty feeling

    As if something is stuck in the eye.

  • Redness and watering

    Often with a discharge or sticky eyelids when there is an infection.

  • Light hurts

    Bright light feels painful or makes you shut the eye.

  • Blurred or hazy vision

    From swelling, a scar or a change in the shape of the cornea.

  • A white spot on the eye

    A white or grey patch on the clear part can be an ulcer or a scar.

  • Glasses power changing fast

    Especially cylinder power in a teenager or young adult, which can be a sign of keratoconus.

Same day

Come the same day if

  • Something hits or enters the eye, or a chemical splashes into it. First wash the eye with plenty of clean water for at least 15 minutes.
  • You wear contact lenses and the eye turns red and painful
  • A white spot appears on the eye, or your sight drops quickly

04Tests

How we check

  1. 01

    Slit lamp examination

    A microscope with a fine beam of light shows each layer of the cornea. A drop of yellow dye lights up scratches and ulcers.

  2. 02

    Corneal topography

    A painless scan that maps the shape and thickness of the cornea. It finds keratoconus early.

  3. 03

    Specular microscopy

    Counts the cells on the inner layer that keep the cornea clear. Useful before cataract surgery or a transplant.

  4. 04

    For a serious infection, a tiny sample is taken with numbing drops, to find the germ and choose the right medicine.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • Infections and inflammation

    Medicines

    Antibiotic, antifungal or antiviral drops, sometimes every hour at first, with drops for pain and dryness. Using them exactly as told is what saves the eye.

  • Keratoconus

    Special contact lenses

    Rigid (RGP), hybrid or scleral lenses smooth out an uneven cornea and give sharp sight when glasses cannot.

  • Keratoconus that is getting worse

    Corneal cross-linking

    Vitamin drops and a measured dose of ultraviolet light stiffen the cornea, so keratoconus stops getting worse. It works best when done early.

  • Pterygium

    Pterygium removal

    The fleshy growth is removed and the area is covered with a thin graft of the eye's own tissue, which lowers the chance of it coming back.

  • Badly scarred or swollen cornea

    Corneal transplant

    The damaged cornea is replaced with a clear donor cornea from an eye bank. Depending on the damage, the full thickness (PK) or only the inner layer (DSEK, DMEK) is replaced.

  4. 4

    Most patients start drops the same day. For an ulcer, you come back often in the first days, so the doctor can see it healing.

07Afterwards

Looking after your cornea

What helps

  • Use every drop exactly as prescribed, and finish the course even if the eye feels better.
  • Do not use steroid drops, old drops or home remedies without a doctor's advice.
  • Do not rub your eyes, especially if you have keratoconus or allergies.
  • If you wear contact lenses, never sleep in them, never rinse them with tap water, and take them out if the eye turns red.
  • Wear protective glasses when working with tools, crops or chemicals.
  • After a transplant, keep every follow-up visit. The new cornea needs drops for many months.

Call the branch if

  • Pain or redness increases
  • Your sight gets worse
  • After a transplant, the eye turns red, sensitive to light or blurred. This can be rejection, which is treatable if caught early.

Questions people ask

Can I treat a red eye with home remedies?

Please do not. Home remedies can carry germs into the eye and turn a small scratch into an ulcer. Wash the eye with clean water and see a doctor.

Can keratoconus be cured?

It cannot be reversed, but cross-linking can stop it getting worse, and special contact lenses give good sight to most people. The earlier it is found, the more sight is saved.

Where does a donor cornea come from?

From people who pledged to donate their eyes after death. The cornea is tested and stored by an eye bank. One donor can give sight to two people.

Will a corneal transplant work for me?

It depends on why you need it. The doctor will explain the chances for your eye, and how long the wait for a donor cornea may be.

Does pterygium always need surgery?

No. A small pterygium can be watched and eased with lubricating drops. Surgery is advised if it grows towards the centre, blurs your sight or keeps getting red.

01What it is

What is diabetic retinopathy?

The retina (आँख का पर्दा) lines the back of the eye and turns light into signals for the brain. It is fed by very fine blood vessels. Years of high blood sugar weaken these vessels, so they leak fluid and blood, or close off.

In the early stage there are small bleeds and spots that you cannot feel or see. Later, fluid can collect in the macula, the centre of the retina that you use for reading and faces, and blur your sight. In the advanced stage, fragile new vessels grow, bleed inside the eye and can pull the retina away.

Anyone with diabetes can get it, whether they take tablets or insulin. The longer you have had diabetes, and the higher your sugar, the higher the risk. Good control slows it down, and timely treatment saves sight in most people.

Higher risk with

  • Diabetes for many years
  • Sugar that stays high (a high HbA1c)
  • High blood pressure
  • High cholesterol
  • Kidney disease from diabetes
  • Pregnancy, in women who already have diabetes
  • Smoking

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • Often nothing at all

    Your sight can be perfect while the retina is already damaged. This is why checks matter.

  • Blurred or wavy vision

    Straight lines look bent, or reading becomes hard, when fluid collects in the centre.

  • Floating spots or strings

    Dark spots, cobwebs or floaters can be small bleeds inside the eye.

  • Dark or empty patches

    Parts of what you look at seem missing or shadowed.

  • Faded colours

    Colours look washed out.

Same day

Call the branch the same day if

  • Your sight suddenly drops in one eye
  • A shower of new floaters or a red haze appears
  • A shadow or curtain spreads across your vision

How we check

  1. 01

    Reading the chart with each eye in turn.

  2. 02

    Retina check with drops

    Drops widen the pupil so the doctor can see the whole retina. Your sight stays blurred for four to six hours, so bring someone with you and do not drive.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • For everyone

    Sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol

    The base of all treatment, done with your diabetes doctor. For many adults the HbA1c target is around 7% or lower, but your doctor will set yours.

  • Swelling in the centre of the retina

    Injections into the eye

    Anti-VEGF medicines or steroids are injected into the numbed eye in a clean room. It takes a few minutes, and is usually repeated every month at first.

  • Leaking spots or new vessels

    Laser treatment

    Laser seals leaking spots, or treats the outer retina so it stops making fragile new vessels. It is done in the clinic and may need more than one sitting.

  • Bleeding or a pulled retina

    Vitrectomy

    An operation to clear blood from inside the eye and release scar tissue that pulls on the retina.

  3. 3

    The examination

    The doctor looks at the whole retina with a bright light and a lens. An OCT scan or photographs may be added.

  4. 4

    You are told the stage of retinopathy and when to come back: once a year if all is well, or sooner if you need treatment.

07Afterwards

Protecting your sight

What helps

  • Have a retina check at least once a year, even if you see well.
  • Keep your sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in the range your doctor advises.
  • Take your diabetes medicines regularly, and do not stop them on your own.
  • Stop smoking.
  • If you have diabetes and become pregnant, have your retina checked early in the pregnancy, and again as advised.
  • After an injection, use any drops given, do not rub the eye, and keep it clean for a few days.

Call the branch if

  • Your sight suddenly drops
  • You see many new floaters or a red haze
  • After an injection, pain, redness or blurring gets worse over the next few days. This is rare but needs treatment the same day.

Questions people ask

I see clearly. Do I still need a retina check?

Yes. Diabetic retinopathy often causes no change in sight until it is advanced. A check with drops is the only way to know.

When should my first check be?

For type 2 diabetes, as soon as it is diagnosed. For type 1, within five years of diagnosis. After that, at least once a year, or as often as the eye doctor advises.

Are the injections painful?

The eye is numbed with drops first, so most people feel only a little pressure for a moment. The eye may feel gritty for a day.

Can new glasses fix it?

No. Glasses correct focus, not damage to the retina. Blurred sight in someone with diabetes needs a retina check.

Will treatment bring my sight back?

Treatment aims to stop further loss. Many people with swelling in the centre see better after injections, but damage that has been there a long time may not fully recover.

01What it is

What is glaucoma?

Your eye is filled with a clear fluid that is made and drained all the time. If it drains too slowly, the pressure inside the eye rises and presses on the optic nerve. Over months and years the nerve fibres die, and the edges of your vision fade first.

Because the centre of vision stays sharp until late, most people notice nothing until a large part of their sight is gone. Glaucoma can also damage the nerve when the eye pressure is normal.

There are two main types. In open angle glaucoma, the drain slowly clogs and there is no pain. In angle closure glaucoma, the drain is narrow and can block suddenly, causing a painful red eye that needs treatment the same day.

More likely with

  • Age over 40
  • Glaucoma in a parent, brother or sister
  • High eye pressure
  • Diabetes, high or low blood pressure, or thyroid disease
  • High minus or high plus glasses power
  • An eye injury or earlier eye surgery
  • Long use of steroid drops, tablets or creams

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • Usually nothing at first

    Open angle glaucoma gives no pain and no early warning. Only an eye check can find it.

  • Side vision fading

    Bumping into things, missing a step, or not seeing someone standing beside you.

  • Rainbow halos around lights

    Coloured rings around bulbs, especially at night.

  • Eye ache or headache

    Especially in the evening or after time in a dark room, in people whose drain is narrow.

Same day

Come the same day if you have

  • Sudden, severe eye pain with a red eye
  • Blurred sight with halos around lights
  • Headache, nausea or vomiting along with the eye pain

This can be an attack of angle closure glaucoma. The pressure has to be brought down within hours to save the sight.

04Tests

How we check

  1. 01

    Eye pressure (tonometry)

    A painless measurement, after numbing drops or with a puff of air.

  2. 02

    Gonioscopy

    A special lens on the numbed eye shows whether the drain is open or narrow.

  3. 03

    Optic nerve check

    Drops widen the pupil, and the doctor looks at the nerve for signs of damage.

  4. 04

    Visual field test

    You press a button each time you see a small light. It maps your side vision, and repeating it shows whether glaucoma is getting worse.

  5. 05

    OCT scan

    A quick, painless scan that measures the layer of nerve fibres, and can show thinning before you notice any change.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • First treatment for most people

    Eye drops

    One or more drops a day lower the pressure. They only work while you use them, so for most people they are for life.

  • Narrow drains, and some open angle glaucoma

    Laser

    A laser makes a tiny opening in the iris (iridotomy) to open a narrow drain, or treats the drain itself (trabeculoplasty) so fluid flows out better. It takes a few minutes in the clinic.

  • When drops and laser are not enough

    Glaucoma surgery

    Trabeculectomy makes a new drain for the fluid. Other operations use a small drainage tube, or newer, gentler methods (MIGS), sometimes together with cataract surgery.

06On the day

A glaucoma check, step by step

  1. 1

    Your history

    Your age, family history, other illnesses, and every medicine you take, including steroids.

  2. 2

    Pressure and drain

    The eye pressure is measured, and the drain is checked with a special lens.

  3. 3

    Nerve and field

    Drops widen the pupil for the nerve check. A visual field test and an OCT scan may be done the same day or on another visit.

  4. 4

    Your plan

    If you have glaucoma, you start treatment with a target pressure. Follow-up is usually every few months, and the tests are repeated to make sure the damage is not growing.

07Afterwards

Living with glaucoma

What helps

  • Use your drops at the same time every day. A phone reminder helps.
  • Do not stop the drops when the bottle runs out or the eye feels fine. Glaucoma does not hurt, even when it is getting worse.
  • After each drop, close the eye and press gently on the inner corner for a minute. More of the medicine stays in the eye.
  • If you use two different drops, wait five minutes between them.
  • Keep every follow-up visit, even when you feel well.
  • Ask your brothers, sisters and children to have their eyes checked.

Call the branch if

  • A drop makes your eye very red, itchy or swollen
  • You get sudden pain, redness or halos
  • You feel breathless or your heartbeat slows after starting a new drop. Some glaucoma drops can affect people with asthma or heart problems.

09Questions

Questions people ask

Can sight lost to glaucoma come back?

No. Treatment cannot repair the nerve, but it can stop or slow further damage. That is why finding glaucoma early matters so much.

Is glaucoma the same as cataract?

No, although people often mix them up. A cataract is a cloudy lens that surgery can fix. Glaucoma is damage to the nerve, which can be controlled but not reversed.

How often should I get checked?

Everyone over 40 should have a glaucoma check as part of an eye check-up. If glaucoma runs in your family, start earlier and repeat it as the doctor advises, often every year.

Will I need drops for life?

Most people do. Some people with a narrow drain are treated with laser alone, and surgery can reduce or end the need for drops in others.

Can glaucoma cause blindness?

Without treatment, it can. With regular treatment and check-ups, most people keep useful sight for life.

01What it is

What is an ICL?

An ICL works like a contact lens that stays inside the eye. It is placed through a tiny cut, behind the coloured iris and just in front of your natural lens, where it cannot be seen or felt.

Unlike LASIK, it does not remove any tissue from the cornea. That makes it an option for people whose power is very high, or whose cornea is too thin for laser surgery.

Your natural lens stays in place. So, like anyone else, you will still need reading glasses in your forties or fifties, and you can still have cataract surgery later in life.

It may suit you if

  • You are roughly 21 to 45 years old
  • Your glasses power has been stable for at least a year
  • Your power is high, or your cornea is too thin for LASIK
  • There is enough space inside the front of your eye (measured at the check-up)
  • Your eyes are otherwise healthy
  • You are not pregnant or breastfeeding

08Questions

Questions people ask

ICL or LASIK: which is better?

Neither is better for everyone. LASIK reshapes the cornea and suits moderate power with a healthy, thick cornea. An ICL suits higher power and thin corneas, and removes no tissue. Your test results decide.

Can the lens be removed?

Yes. An ICL can be taken out or exchanged if needed, for example when you have cataract surgery later in life.

Will I feel the lens?

No. It sits inside the eye where there are no touch nerves, and it cannot be seen from outside.

Will I still need reading glasses?

Probably, from your forties or fifties, like everyone else. The ICL corrects your glasses power, but it does not stop the natural ageing of the eye's focusing.

What are the risks?

Serious problems are uncommon. Possible risks include raised eye pressure, glare or halos at night, an early cataract and infection. The doctor will go through them with you before you decide.

Retinal Detachment

In a retinal detachment, the retina, the seeing layer at the back of the eye, comes away from the wall of the eye. It is an emergency. Repaired in time, most retinas can be put back in place and sight saved.

Flashes, a shower of floaters or a shadow? These need an eye check the same day. Call the branch now and tell them what you are seeing.

01What it is

What is a retinal detachment?

The retina (आँख का पर्दा) is a thin layer that lines the inside of the back of the eye, like wallpaper. When it peels away, it stops working, and the part of your vision it served goes dark.

It usually starts with a small tear. As we get older, the jelly that fills the eye shrinks and can tug on the retina, causing flashes and floaters. Fluid then passes through the tear and lifts the retina off. Less often, scar tissue from diabetes pulls it away.

A tear caught early can often be sealed with laser in the clinic. Once the retina has detached, surgery is needed, and the sooner it is done, the better the chance of good sight, especially while the centre of the retina is still attached.

More likely with

  • High minus glasses power (short sight)
  • A detachment in the other eye before
  • Retinal detachment in the family
  • A hard blow to the eye or head
  • Earlier eye surgery, including cataract surgery
  • Advanced diabetic retinopathy
  • Age over 50

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • Flashes of light

    Brief flickers or streaks of light at the edge of vision, often easier to notice in the dark.

  • A shower of new floaters

    Many new black dots, cobwebs or a smoky haze, appearing suddenly.

  • A shadow or curtain

    A dark shadow spreading in from the side, top or bottom of your vision.

  • Blurred or wavy vision

    Straight lines look bent, or the centre goes blurred, when the middle of the retina is affected.

Same day

No pain does not mean no problem

A retinal detachment does not hurt. Do not wait to see if it settles. Call the branch the same day, and avoid heavy work until you have been seen.

Call Patna branch now

03How it can look

How it can look

Our Patna branch, as it may look to someone with this problem. Drag the handle to compare.

04Tests

How we check

  1. 01

    Retina check with drops

    Drops widen the pupil, and the doctor examines the whole retina, pressing gently on the eyelid to see the far edges.

  2. 02

    OCT scan

    Shows whether the centre of the retina (the macula) is still attached.

  3. 03

    Ultrasound (B-scan)

    If blood or a cataract blocks the view, sound waves show whether the retina is in place.

  4. 04

    Retina photographs

    Record where the tears and the detachment are.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • A tear, before it detaches

    Laser or freezing for a tear

    Laser, or a freezing probe, seals the edges of the tear so fluid cannot get under the retina. It takes a few minutes in the clinic.

  • Some small detachments

    Pneumatic retinopexy

    A gas bubble is injected into the eye to press the retina back into place, and the tear is then sealed with laser or freezing.

  • Some detachments, often in younger people

    Scleral buckle

    A soft band is stitched to the outside wall of the eye to push it against the tear. It stays in place for good and cannot be seen.

  • Most detachments

    Vitrectomy

    The jelly is removed, the retina is flattened and the tears are sealed with laser. The eye is then filled with gas, which slowly disappears, or with silicone oil, which is removed in a second operation a few months later.

From your call to surgery

    Call the branch

    Tell them you have flashes, floaters or a shadow. You will be asked to come in the same day.

  2. 2

    Examination

    Drops widen your pupil and the retina is examined, with a scan if needed. Come with someone, as your sight will be blurred.

  3. 3

    Treatment

    A tear may be treated with laser the same day. A detachment needs surgery as soon as possible, often within a day or two. The doctor explains which operation suits your eye.

  4. 4

    After the operation

    If gas was used, you may need to keep your head in a set position for several days. This keeps the bubble pressing on the tear, and it matters as much as the operation.

07Afterwards

After surgery

What helps

  • Keep the head position you were given, for as many hours a day as you were told.
  • With gas in the eye, do not fly or travel up into the hills until the doctor says the gas has gone. The bubble swells with height and can raise the eye pressure dangerously.
  • With gas in the eye, tell any doctor who plans to give you an anaesthetic about it first.
  • Use the drops as prescribed, and wear the shield at night.
  • Avoid heavy lifting and bending until the doctor says it is safe.
  • Sight improves slowly, over weeks to months. Your glasses power is checked again later.

Call the branch if

  • Pain gets worse, or you start vomiting
  • Your sight gets worse after first improving
  • You see new flashes, floaters or a shadow in either eye

09Questions

Questions people ask

Can a retinal detachment heal on its own?

No. Without treatment, a detached retina usually stays detached, and the eye can lose its sight for good.

Is every floater a sign of detachment?

No. Most people have a few floaters, and they are harmless. What matters is a sudden change: many new floaters, flashes or a shadow. That needs a check the same day.

Will my sight come back fully?

It depends on how long the retina was detached and whether the centre was affected. Many people get good reading sight back, but it can take months, and some blur may remain.

Can it happen in the other eye?

It can, so the doctor checks the other eye as well. Know the warning signs, and act quickly if they appear.

How long will I need to keep my head down?

Usually from a few days to a week or two, depending on the gas used and where the tear is. The doctor will tell you exactly.

ROP Retinopathy of Prematurity

ROP is an eye problem in babies born early or small. The blood vessels of the retina have not finished growing, and in some babies they grow the wrong way. It cannot be seen from outside, so babies at risk need eye screening by an eye doctor in the first weeks of life.

Born before 34 weeks, or under 2 kg? Ask your baby's doctor when the eye screening is due, then call us to book it. Please do not miss the date.

01What it is

What is ROP?

In the womb, the blood vessels of the retina grow slowly, and finish close to the due date. When a baby is born early, this growth is not complete. In some babies the vessels then grow abnormally. This is retinopathy of prematurity.

Mild ROP often settles by itself as the baby grows. Severe ROP can pull the retina away and cause blindness. There are no outward signs, and a baby cannot tell you, so the only way to find it is a screening by an eye doctor.

When ROP needs treatment, it has to be done quickly, usually within two to three days of being found. Treated in time, most babies keep their sight.

Which babies need screening

  • Born before 34 weeks of pregnancy
  • Weighed less than 2,000 g (2 kg) at birth
  • Bigger babies who had a difficult stay in the newborn unit (NICU), for example long oxygen treatment, a serious infection or breathing problems

The first screening is due within the first month after birth, and sooner for babies born very early or very small. Your baby's doctor will give you the date.

02Signs

What parents may notice

  • Usually nothing

    ROP cannot be seen from outside in its early stages. Screening is the only way to find it.

  • A white pupil

    In very advanced ROP the pupil can look white. This needs urgent attention.

  • Not following faces or lights

    By about three months after the due date, babies should look at faces and follow them.

  • Eyes that wander or shake

    Later on, poor sight can show as a squint or wobbly eye movements.

03Tests

How babies are checked

  1. 01

    Eye screening

    After drops widen the pupils, the eye doctor looks at the retina with a head-mounted light and a hand lens. A tiny clip keeps the eyelids open. It takes a few minutes for each eye.

  2. 02

    Repeat screening

    Depending on what is found, the check is repeated every one to two weeks until the vessels finish growing.

  3. 03

    Eye checks in childhood

    Babies born early have a higher chance of squint, lazy eye and high glasses power, so their eyes are checked as they grow.

04Treatment

Treatment options

  • Mild ROP

    Watching closely

    Most mild ROP settles on its own. The baby is screened again regularly until the retina has finished developing.

  • ROP that needs treatment

    Laser treatment

    Laser is applied to the outer retina, where vessels have not grown, so the abnormal vessels stop growing. It is done with the baby under anaesthesia or sedation.

  • Some severe ROP

    Injection into the eye

    A medicine (anti-VEGF) injected into the eye stops the abnormal growth. Babies treated this way need a longer period of follow-up.

  • Detached retina

    Surgery

    In advanced ROP, an operation may be needed to put the retina back in place.

Ayushman card and insurance

All three branches accept the Ayushman card (PM-JAY), and cashless treatment works with most insurance TPAs. Call the branch to check what is covered for your treatment.

05On the day

The screening visit

  1. 1

    Before the check

    Drops to widen the pupils go in about an hour before. The nurse or doctor will tell you about feeding before the check.

  2. 2

    The screening

    Numbing drops, a small clip to hold the eyelids open, and a few minutes of looking with a bright light. Babies often cry, but it does not harm the eye.

  3. 3

    Afterwards

    The eyelids may look puffy and red for a few hours. Your baby can feed, and go home or back to the newborn unit as usual.

  4. 4

    The next date

    You are told the result and the date of the next check. Please keep it, even if your baby has gone home.

06Afterwards

After screening or treatment

What helps

  • Keep every screening date. Missing one can mean missing the time when treatment works.
  • If your baby leaves hospital before screening is finished, ask for the next date and place before you go.
  • After treatment, use any drops exactly as prescribed.
  • Have your child's eyes checked regularly through childhood, even after ROP has settled.

Call the branch if

  • The eyes become very red, swollen or sticky after treatment
  • You notice a white pupil, or the eyes do not seem to follow you
  • You miss a screening date. Call to book again straight away.

08Questions

Questions people ask

Does my baby need screening if the eyes look normal?

Yes. ROP cannot be seen from outside. Babies with severe ROP can have eyes that look completely normal.

Is the screening painful?

It is uncomfortable and most babies cry, but numbing drops are used, and it takes only a few minutes. It does not harm the eyes.

When can screening stop?

When the eye doctor sees that the blood vessels have grown fully to the edge of the retina, or that ROP has settled. This is usually some weeks after the original due date.

Will my baby need glasses?

Some babies born early need glasses later, even without ROP. Regular eye checks in childhood will find this.

Our baby has already gone home. What now?

Call the branch to book the screening, and bring the discharge papers. If you are not sure when it is due, ask your baby's doctor.

Squint भेंगापन

A squint is when the two eyes do not point in the same direction. One eye may turn in, out, up or down, all the time or only now and then. In children it should be checked early, because it can lead to a lazy eye. In adults it can cause double vision and strain.

01What it is

What is a squint?

Each eye is moved by six small muscles. To see one clear picture, the muscles of both eyes have to work together. When they do not, the eyes point in different directions. Doctors call this strabismus.

In a child, the brain starts to ignore the picture from the turned eye. That eye can then lose sight for good, which is called amblyopia, or lazy eye. Children do not grow out of a true squint, so the earlier it is checked, the better the result.

In adults, a squint can be left over from childhood or start new, for example after nerve damage from diabetes or blood pressure, thyroid eye disease or an injury. A new squint with double vision needs to be checked soon.

More likely with

  • A squint or lazy eye in the family
  • Being born early or very small
  • High glasses power, especially plus power
  • Cerebral palsy, Down syndrome and some other conditions
  • In adults: diabetes, high blood pressure, thyroid eye disease or a head injury

02Signs

Signs to watch for

  • An eye that turns

    In, out, up or down. It may show only when the child is tired, unwell or looking far away.

  • Tilting or turning the head

    To use the eyes together more comfortably.

  • Closing one eye

    Especially in bright sunlight.

  • Double vision

    Mostly in adults and older children.

  • Eye strain or headaches

    After reading or time on a screen.

  • Clumsiness

    Poor judgement of depth: missing a step or a catch.

Same day

Get checked the same day if

  • Double vision or a squint appears suddenly
  • It comes with a headache, a drooping eyelid, or weakness or numbness anywhere in the body

04Tests

How we check

  1. 01

    Vision test for each eye

    With pictures or letters to suit the child's age.

  2. 02

    Glasses power with drops

    Drops relax the eye's focusing to find the true glasses power. They take up to an hour to work and blur near sight for some hours.

  3. 03

    Squint measurement

    The doctor covers each eye in turn and uses prisms to measure how much the eye turns, up close and at a distance.

  4. 04

    Eye movements and 3D vision

    How the eyes move together, and how well they judge depth.

  5. 05

    Eye health check

    To make sure nothing inside the eye, such as a cataract, is causing the squint.

05Treatment

Treatment options

  • Often the first step

    Glasses

    In some children, glasses alone straighten the eyes, because the squint is caused by high power. They need to be worn all day.

  • If a lazy eye has developed

    Patching

    Covering the stronger eye for some hours a day makes the weaker eye work. This comes before any surgery.

  • Some types only

    Eye exercises

    Exercises (orthoptics) help when the eyes drift outward while reading, as in convergence insufficiency. They do not correct most squints.

  • When the turn remains

    Squint surgery

    The eye muscles are moved or tightened to straighten the eyes. Nothing is cut on the face, and the eye is never taken out. Children have it under general anaesthesia, and most go home the same day.

  • Some patients

    Botulinum injection

    A small injection weakens an eye muscle for some weeks or months. It is used for some adults and young children, instead of or before surgery.

Ayushman card and insurance

All three branches accept the Ayushman card (PM-JAY), and cashless treatment works with most insurance TPAs. Call the branch to check what is covered for your treatment.

06On the day

If your child needs squint surgery

  1. 1

    Before the day

    A check by the doctor and the anaesthetist, and clear instructions on when your child must stop eating and drinking.

  2. 2

    The operation

    Your child is asleep under general anaesthesia. The operation usually takes 30 to 60 minutes.

  3. 3

    Waking up

    You can be with your child as they wake. The eye will be red and a little sore.

  4. 4

    Going home

    Usually the same day, with drops. Most children are back at school within a week.

  5. 5

    Follow-up

    Checks over the following weeks. Glasses or patching often continue after surgery.

07Afterwards

After squint surgery

What helps

  • Use the drops as prescribed. The redness fades over two to three weeks.
  • Keep dirty water and dust out of the eye, and no swimming for two weeks.
  • Do not rub the eye. Children may need gentle reminders.
  • Keep wearing glasses and patches as advised. Surgery straightens the eyes, but it does not replace them.
  • Some people need a second operation later. This is common, and it does not mean the first one failed.

Call the branch if

  • Pain, swelling or discharge increases
  • Your child has a fever or seems unwell
  • Sight in the operated eye drops

09Questions

Questions people ask

Will my child grow out of a squint?

No. A true squint does not go away by itself, and waiting can cause a lazy eye. A baby's eyes can wander now and then in the first three to four months, but a squint after that age should be checked.

My baby's eyes look crossed in photos. Is that a squint?

Sometimes a broad, flat nose bridge makes straight eyes look crossed. The doctor can tell the difference with a simple check.

Is it too late for an adult?

No. Adults can have squint surgery to straighten the eyes, and in many cases it also eases double vision and helps the eyes work together.

Will my child still need glasses after surgery?

Often, yes. Surgery corrects the position of the eyes, and glasses correct the power. Many children need both.

Is squint surgery safe?

It is a common, well established operation. Like any surgery it has risks, such as the eye ending up slightly over or under corrected, which the doctor will explain.
